author: BBC News
description:
Companies are offering to help migrants pose as talented artists and tech experts to make fraudulent UK visa applications under a fast-track immigration scheme, the BBC has found.
 
The UK government's Global Talent visa was launched in 2020 to attract the "brightest and best" scientists and researchers from around the world. It is also open to creative artists.
 
Following our investigation, the Home Office is now revoking visas issued to two Nigerian men who claimed to be fine art photographers, because it believes they were obtained by deception.

author: BBC News
description:
All flights in the US have been grounded due to "extraordinary circumstances" relating to air traffic control communication issues. 

US Federal Aviation Administration  issued an order to ground all flights due "for reasons of safety”.

The US Transport Secretary Sean Duffy said the issue had hit air traffic control centres and "FAA technicians are investigating the issue. We will provide immediate updates as we have them”.

The US Secretary for Homeland Security has said there is no indication of any kind of threat to the United States and the emergency is not due to a cyber attack. 

The emergency is having an enormous impact on flights across the United States, with thousands of flights in the air and many more scheduled to depart in the coming hours. 

Passengers are being advised to check their flight status directly with their airline.

Jane Hill presents BBC News at Ten reporting by Sarah Smith in Washington. 

Subscribe to our channel here: https://bbc.in/bbcnews

The UN nuclear watchdog has said it is increasingly concerned about Iran's uranium enrichment plant at Isfahan.
 
The International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) said it does not know the exact location or whether the facility contains nuclear material.
 
The IAEA believes much of Iran's highly enriched uranium was stored there.
 
Meanwhile, the US military has denied Iranian claims that they've destroyed a US early-warning radar system in Bahrain.

After former entertainer Russell Brand was sentenced to 10-and-a-half-years in jail for one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault earlier this week, a corner of social media is pushing false claims and conspiracy theories in support of him.

description:
Microsoft says it is seeing sustained improvements in service availability after an outage saw users in more than 70 countries lose access to Outlook email and calendar services, Teams chat and CoPilot AI software. Microsoft says it has not found any evidence that malicious activity caused the problems.

In this video, we find out what may have caused the Microsoft outage, and how vulnerable we are to another one. We also ask a cybersecurity expert what lessons we can learn about digital resilience, and a mindfulness teacher tells us why disconnecting from email could be good for our mental health.

description:
“This is the biggest entertainment release ever”, says the BBC’s technology reporter, Laura Cress. 
 
Like the 10 million people who have pre-ordered Grand Theft Auto 6 ahead of its launch on 19 November, Laura is excited to experience the ground-breaking graphics and new features - including the first female protagonist - of gaming’s biggest franchise.
 
Laura tells The Global Story’s Tristan Redman about GTA’s surprising roots - in a small studio in Dundee, Scotland - and explains how its nihilistic eye on the US cities the game is modelled on has courted controversy and raised political debate.

author: BBC News
description:
These hidden World War Two plotting rooms were buried and forgotten until they were rediscovered by the National Trust in 2017.
 
The Fan Bay Plotting Room, beneath the White Cliffs of Dover, housed pioneering military technology during the war.
 
In 1940, with the Germans threatening invasion, Winston Churchill ordered the building of secret tunnels to control the guns that would be the first line of defence. 
 
After years of work by volunteers and The National Trust, the underground room has been rediscovered under tonnes of soil and will open to the public.

author: BBC News
description:
School is one of the great unquestioned assumptions of childhood. It’s where children go to learn, make friends and prepare for adult life. But what if the conventional classroom isn’t the best place for every child to thrive? And what if some children would be better off without school altogether?

Developmental psychologist Naomi Fisher believes that school is not the best, or the only, way for children to get a good education. She joins Gabriel Gatehouse to make the case for homeschooling and ‘unschooling’, arguing that many children can learn best when they’re free to follow their interests rather than a prescribed curriculum.

From children teaching themselves to read through Minecraft to the question of whether traditional schooling can prepare the next generation for an AI-driven world, Fisher challenges some of our assumptions about education, achievement, and childhood.
